summary: Discusses implementation issues when providing compulsory tunneling in dial-up networks, where the network operator rather than the user sets up an L2TP tunnel, with RADIUS used for authentication and configuration. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Compulsory tunnelling is where the network operator, not the caller, decides that a connection should be carried inside a tunnel to a particular destination. This memo explains how a dial-up provider does that: the access server asks a RADIUS server about the caller, the reply names the tunnel endpoint to use, and the access server then sets up the L2TP tunnel and hands the call over. The tunnel server completes the PPP setup and assigns the address.

subtitle: How a dial-up provider sends every caller down a private tunnel it chose for them, and how RADIUS tells it where to send them.

tldr.problem: Some services need their users to reach one specific host and nothing else. A provider can do that by sending every caller down a private tunnel, but it needs a way to decide, per caller, which tunnel endpoint to use, and a way to authenticate the caller along the way.
tldr.mechanism: The access server asks a RADIUS server about the caller. The RADIUS reply carries tunnel attributes, and the access server then builds an L2TP tunnel to the tunnel server named there, which finishes the PPP negotiation and assigns the address.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Informational and describes how to put RADIUS and L2TP together. It compares single and dual authentication, gives the start-up and tear-down sequences, and sets out the security rules that the RADIUS proxies and the access server must follow.

today: RFC 2809 is an Informational memo from April 2000 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes how to combine RADIUS with tunnelling, and it depends on the L2TP and RADIUS specifications of its time, RFC 2661 and RFC 2138, and on a separate work in progress for the RADIUS attributes that carry the tunnelling information.

sections.title: Why Compulsory Tunneling, and Why RADIUS
sections.content:
Many applications of tunnelling protocols involve dial-up network access. Some, such as providing secure access to corporate intranets via the Internet, are characterised by voluntary tunneling, where the tunnel is created at the request of the user for a specific purpose. Others involve compulsory tunneling, where the tunnel is created without any action from the user and without allowing the user any choice.

Examples of applications that might be implemented using compulsory tunnels are Internet software upgrade servers, software registration servers and banking services. These are services which, without compulsory tunnelling, would probably be provided using dedicated networks or at least dedicated network access servers, because they are characterised by the need to limit user access to specific hosts.

Given the widespread support for compulsory tunnelling, these types of services could be accessed via any Internet service provider. The most popular means of authorising dial-up network users today is through the RADIUS protocol, and the use of RADIUS allows the authorisation and authentication data to be maintained in a central location rather than on each access server. It makes sense to use RADIUS to centrally administer compulsory tunnelling, since RADIUS is widely deployed and was designed to carry this type of information. New RADIUS attributes are needed to carry the tunnelling information from the RADIUS server to the access server; those attributes are defined in a separate work in progress, not in this document.

The memo argues for RADIUS-based, user-based tunnelling over two alternatives. Static tunnelling sends all users to a given endpoint, and requires a dedicated access server for the purpose; in the case of an ISP that is undesirable, because it means dedicating a device to one customer rather than using existing access servers, and it is likely to be costly to deploy as a global service. Realm-based tunnelling picks the endpoint from the realm part of the user name, which assumes that all users within a given realm wish to be treated the same way and so limits flexibility in account management. The memo's example is of a company that wants one employee to have an account giving access to both the Internet and an intranet, with the intranet access provided by a tunnel server in the engineering department, and another employee to have an account giving only intranet access, with that provided by a tunnel server in the sales department. Realm-based tunnelling cannot accommodate that, but user-based tunnelling can.
sections.plainLanguage: Two simpler designs exist: send everybody to the same tunnel endpoint, or send everybody whose user name ends in the same suffix to the same endpoint. Both are inflexible. With RADIUS, the provider can decide separately for each account where that person should be sent, so one employee reaches one tunnel server and another reaches a different one, while the provider keeps one list of accounts in one place.

sections.title: The Pieces
sections.content:
Four roles appear throughout the document.

  • The Network Access Server (NAS) is the device that clients contact in order to get access to the network. In L2TP terminology, a NAS performing compulsory tunnelling is referred to as the L2TP Access Concentrator (LAC).
  • The tunnel server terminates the tunnel. In L2TP terminology this is the L2TP Network Server (LNS).
  • The RADIUS authentication server provides authentication and authorisation using the protocol described in RFC 2138.
  • The RADIUS proxy routes RADIUS authentication requests. To the NAS it appears to act as a RADIUS server, and to the RADIUS server it appears to act as a RADIUS client. It can be used to locate the tunnel endpoint when realm-based tunnelling is used.

The tunnel protocol discussed here is L2TP, defined in RFC 2661. Implementation issues encountered with other tunnelling protocols are left to separate documents.
sections.plainLanguage: The caller dials the access server, the device that gives people access to the network. The access server asks a RADIUS server, which checks the caller's details and returns a reply. If the reply carries tunnel attributes, the access server sets up an L2TP tunnel to the tunnel server named there, and the call continues inside that tunnel.

sections.title: Single and Dual Authentication
sections.content:
RADIUS-based compulsory tunnelling can support both single authentication, where the user is authenticated at the NAS or the tunnel server, and dual authentication, where the user is authenticated at both the NAS and the tunnel server.

Single authentication has three variants.

  • NAS authentication. Authentication and authorisation, including the tunnelling information, occurs once, at the NAS. This disallows network access for unauthorised NAS users and permits accounting to be done at the NAS. Its disadvantages are that the tunnel server must trust the NAS, since no user authentication occurs there, and that accounting cannot take place at the tunnel server with strong assurance that the correct party is being billed. It is most typically used with LCP forwarding and tunnel authentication, both supported in L2TP, so the tunnel server can accept all calls within authenticated tunnels without requiring PPP authentication. It is not compatible with roaming, since the tunnel server will typically only accept tunnels from a restricted set of access servers.
  • NAS authentication with RADIUS reply forwarding. Authentication and authorisation occurs once at the NAS and the RADIUS reply is forwarded to the tunnel server. This disallows network access for unauthorised NAS users, does not require trust between the NAS and the tunnel server, and allows accounting at both ends. However it requires that both ends share the same secret with the RADIUS server, since that is the only way the tunnel server can check the Access-Reply. While this can work if the reply comes directly from a RADIUS server, it becomes unmanageable if a RADIUS proxy is involved, because the reply would be authenticated with the secret shared by the client and the proxy rather than by the RADIUS server. The memo therefore calls this scheme impractical.
  • Tunnel server authentication. Authentication and authorisation occurs once at the tunnel server. The NAS has to determine first that the user needs to be tunnelled, through RADIUS or through its own configuration. With RADIUS, the determination can be made from the telephone-number based attributes, the Calling-Station-Id and Called-Station-Id, or from the userID, such as its domain portion.

Dual authentication means the user is authenticated at both ends. Its advantages are authentication and accounting at both ends of the tunnel, the use of a single userID and password pair because the tunnel server also speaks RADIUS, and no need for telephone-number based authentication or attribute-specific processing on the RADIUS server. It also produces accounting records on both sides, making auditing possible, and the tunnel endpoint does not need an account relationship with the owner of the access server, so the scheme is compatible with roaming. Its disadvantage is that LCP will need to be renegotiated unless LCP forwarding is used; some clients do not support renegotiation at all, and others support only a subset of the dual authentication combinations. The feasible combinations are PAP/PAP(token), PAP/CHAP, PAP/EAP, CHAP/PAP(token), CHAP/CHAP, CHAP/EAP, EAP/CHAP and EAP/EAP.
sections.plainLanguage: The caller can be authenticated once, at the access server or at the tunnel server, or twice, once at each. Authenticating twice means both ends can record who was billed, and the tunnel server does not have to trust the access server. It also means the caller goes through the sign-in process twice, and some client software cannot manage that.

sections.title: Setting Up and Tearing Down the Tunnel
sections.content:
With dual authentication, the sequence is as follows. The client and the NAS begin LCP negotiation, then PPP authentication, and the NAS sends a RADIUS Access-Request to the RADIUS server, which answers with an Access-Accept carrying tunnel attributes or an Access-Reject. If a tunnel is indicated, the NAS brings up an L2TP control connection if none existed before, and the NAS and tunnel server bring up the call with an Incoming-Call-Request, an Incoming-Call-Reply and an Incoming-Call-Connected. Data then flows through the tunnel. The client and the tunnel server may renegotiate LCP and go through another round of PPP authentication, and the tunnel server may send a RADIUS Access-Request of its own. Finally the client and the tunnel server begin NCP negotiation, and the tunnel server assigns the address.

Two rules govern the handover. Because address assignment happens at the tunnel server, the NAS SHOULD NOT send an LCP CONFACK that completes LCP negotiation; instead it sends an LCP Configure-Request, so the client MAY renegotiate LCP and from that point forward all PPP packets from the client are encapsulated and sent to the tunnel server. And the client and the NAS MUST NOT begin NCP negotiation, because that could let the client send packets out to the open network, which compulsory tunnelling does not permit. In single authentication compulsory tunnelling, L2TP authentication forwarding MUST NOT be employed. Where user-based tunnelling via RADIUS is implemented, L2TP authentication forwarding SHOULD NOT be employed either, because that facility creates a vulnerability to replay attacks and causes problems when the NAS and the tunnel server authenticate against different RADIUS servers.

Tear-down is nearly the same in every case. If the client ends the session, the tunnel server MUST terminate the PPP session and then send a Call-Clear-Request to the NAS, and the NAS MUST answer with a Call-Disconnect-Notify and disconnect the call. If the NAS receives a Call-Clear-Request from the tunnel server without a client-requested termination, it MUST respond with a Call-Disconnect-Notify and disconnect. If there is a line problem or a user hangup, the NAS MUST send a Call-Disconnect-Notify to the tunnel server, and both sides tear the call down. If the access is rejected, or the control connection or call setup reports an error, the NAS MUST send an LCP-Terminate and disconnect the user.
sections.plainLanguage: The access server asks RADIUS about the caller, sets up the L2TP tunnel and the call, and passes the caller's PPP packets through it. The tunnel server then renegotiates PPP with the caller and assigns the address. When the call ends, both sides exchange the L2TP teardown messages and close the tunnel. The rule that matters is that the caller must not be able to send to the open network before reaching the tunnel server, so network address negotiation does not start until the tunnel is up.

sections.title: Distinct RADIUS Servers and UserIDs
sections.content:
When the NAS and the tunnel server use distinct RADIUS servers, distinct userID and password pairs are likely to be required: one pair for the initial PPP authentication with the NAS and a second for the authentication at the tunnel server. That has implications if the NAS attempts to forward authentication information to the tunnel server in the initial setup notification, because the pair used for tunnel authentication differs from the one used against the NAS, so forwarding it in this manner will cause the tunnel authentication to fail. As a result, where user-based tunnelling via RADIUS is implemented, L2TP authentication forwarding SHOULD NOT be employed.

To make the case where the two pairs are identical as easy as possible, tunnel clients typically attempt authentication with the same userID and password pair as was used in the initial PPP negotiation, and only prompt the user for the second pair after that has failed. Rather than putting up an error message indicating an authentication failure, it is preferable to present a dialog requesting the tunnel userID and password combination. The same issue arises with extended authentication methods such as EAP, where one-time passwords or cryptographic calculators mean a different password is used for the first and the second authentication, so the user has to be prompted for the second password.

Multilink PPP raises a further question. The two RADIUS servers may return different Port-Limit attributes. If the NAS's server grants a single channel while the tunnel's server grants more, the correct behaviour is for the tunnel client to open a connection to another NAS in order to bring up a multilink bundle on the tunnel server, and the client MUST NOT indicate to that NAS that the additional link is part of a multilink bundle, which is only indicated in the later negotiation with the tunnel server. If the NAS's server allows more channels than the tunnel's server, the client should terminate use of the excess channels.

The memo notes that using RADIUS relieves the userID from having to do double duty. Rather than being used both for routing the RADIUS authentication and authorisation request and for determining the tunnel endpoint, the userID is now used solely for routing the RADIUS request, and the tunnel attributes returned in the RADIUS Access-Response determine the tunnel endpoint. Where RADIUS proxies and tunnelling are employed, it is possible to let the user authenticate with a single userID and password pair at both ends, by routing the NAS's Access-Request to the same RADIUS server the tunnel server uses.
sections.plainLanguage: If the access server and the tunnel server keep separate lists of users, the caller will probably have to give two different passwords, and the system should ask for the second one rather than simply saying no. The user name also stops having to do two jobs: it now only says which RADIUS server should handle the request, and the tunnel attributes in the reply say where the caller should be sent.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
In PPP-based tunnelling, PPP security is negotiated between the client and the tunnel server and covers the entire length of the path, because the client has no way of knowing that it is being tunnelled. Any security the NAS may negotiate with the tunnel server therefore occurs in addition to that negotiated between the client and the NAS. In L2TP compulsory tunnelling this means PPP encryption and compression are negotiated between the client and the tunnel server. In addition, the NAS may bring up an IPsec security association between itself and the tunnel server, which adds protection against a number of possible attacks.

Where RADIUS proxies are deployed, the Access-Reply sent by the RADIUS server may be processed by one or more proxies before the NAS receives it. To ensure that tunnel attributes arrive without modification, intermediate RADIUS proxies forwarding the Access-Reply MUST NOT modify tunnel attributes. If a RADIUS proxy does not support tunnel attributes, it MUST send an Access-Reject to the NAS, so that access is only granted if the services requested by the RADIUS server can be provided.

Since RADIUS tunnel attributes are used for compulsory tunnelling, address assignment is handled by the tunnel server rather than the NAS. If tunnel attributes are present, the NAS MUST ignore any address assignment attributes sent by the RADIUS server. In addition, the NAS and the client MUST NOT begin NCP negotiation, since this could create a time window in which the client is capable of sending packets to the transport network, which is not permitted in compulsory tunnelling.
sections.plainLanguage: Nobody in the middle may change the instructions for where to send the caller, and a proxy that cannot carry those instructions must refuse the request rather than quietly drop it. The caller must also not be let loose on the open network before reaching the place it was sent to, which is why the address is assigned only at the far end.

viz.caption: THE SECURITY RULES THE RFC SETS OUT

items.title: Proxies must not change tunnel attributes
items.text: A proxy forwarding the Access-Reply must leave the tunnel attributes alone.

items.title: Unsupported proxies must reject
items.text: A proxy without tunnel support must send an Access-Reject to the NAS.

items.title: No address assignment at the NAS
items.text: The NAS must ignore RADIUS address attributes when tunnel attributes are present.

items.title: No NCP negotiation yet
items.text: The NAS and client must not start NCP, or the client could reach the transport network.

items.title: PPP security end to end
items.text: Encryption and compression are negotiated between the client and the tunnel server.

items.title: Optional IPsec between NAS and tunnel server
items.text: The NAS may set up an IPsec security association for extra protection.
